title: Medical questions
hook: modern fiqh on transplants, IVF, end of life, where scholars reason and differ

segments.voice: Yesterday, animals' rights, and your line: they have rights. A camel complained in a garden, and the Prophet heard it. Did you check on a creature that couldn't ask? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

Brain-dead. A doctor says the word to a family in a hospital corridor, late at night, about their father, and asks gently whether they would consider donating his kidneys. A few floors up, a young couple is talking with a fertility clinic. In a room at the end of the hall, a grandmother's machines are keeping her body going after her doctors say they can no longer help. None of these questions are in the Qur'an by name. The jurists of Baghdad and Cordoba never saw a ventilator. And yet a Muslim family in that corridor might reach for a phone and ask a scholar: what does the law say? Today: an old method, and questions no one could have asked before.
screen: `A HOSPITAL CORRIDOR AT NIGHT.` → `DONATION, FERTILITY, MACHINES.` → `NONE OF IT NAMED IN THE TEXT.`

segments.voice: Start with medicine itself. In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says that God has not sent down a disease without also sending down its cure. Seeking treatment is part of the tradition, not a lack of trust. Then the method. When a new question comes, scholars look for a text that speaks to it, then reason by analogy from cases that do appear, and weigh the purposes of the law, which we'll meet in two days. That effort of reasoning is called ijtihad. Now the questions. Organ transplants: some fiqh councils have allowed donation, within limits, reading it through the verse in surah five that whoever saves a life, it is as if he had saved all of humankind. Other scholars have objected, out of reverence for the body after death, which the tradition protects. Fertility treatment: Sunni councils have allowed IVF between a married couple, using their own egg and sperm, and refused a third party's. Some Shia authorities have reasoned more widely, allowing some forms of donation. Same texts, different reasoning, both careful. End of life: the same verse in surah five likens killing one soul to killing all humankind, and scholars read it as forbidding a deliberately ended life. Some, though, allow a team to stop treatment that only prolongs dying, when doctors judge there is no hope of recovery, and the question of brain death is still argued. So the answer to a medical question is often not one fatwa but a few, each showing its reasoning. That's not confusion. It's an old method, honestly applied, to new questions.
screen: `GOD SENT A CURE WITH EVERY DISEASE.` · `IJTIHAD: TEXT, ANALOGY, PURPOSE.` · `TRANSPLANTS AND IVF: COUNCILS DIFFER.` · `END OF LIFE: NO KILLING, SOME LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: Reading a modern fatwa takes longer than this sit, so start the way a scholar starts: with the question. Think of one medical decision someone you love has faced, or might. Name it plainly: donation, a treatment, a hard ending. Then ask the three questions from today. Is there a text? Is there a case like it? What is the law trying to protect here? Later, you can look up one fatwa on it and notice how it reasons. For now, hold the person and the question side by side. The bell holds the time.
Medical questions. New cases in medicine, from transplants to fertility to the end of life, that scholars answer by reasoning from the old sources, and on which they sometimes differ. Today's word.

Your line: old method, new questions. Today, when a new problem lands on you, ask what the old principles you trust would say about it. Tomorrow, the law's own word about ease. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Muslim patients and families facing questions about transplants, fertility treatment or end-of-life care may ask a trusted scholar or consult the rulings of fiqh councils, which reason from the Qur'an, the hadith and the purposes of the law.

fork.setup: you're a scholar asked about kidney donation after death. there's no verse about kidneys. what's your first move?
options: refuse to answer, since the text is silent.
reason from texts, similar cases and the law's purposes.
fork.reveal: that's ijtihad; fiqh councils reasoned from 5:32 and allowed donation within limits, while others objected out of respect for the body.

notes: 5:32 paraphrased; Pickthall's wording is 'whoso saveth the life of one, it shall be as if he had saved the life of all mankind'; not quoted to be safe.
Transplants: 'many fiqh councils have allowed' (e.g. OIC Islamic Fiqh Academy 1988, Saudi Council of Senior Scholars); confirm. Objectors exist; confirm fair.
IVF: Sunni councils (e.g. Al-Azhar) allow within marriage, no third party; some Shia authorities (e.g. a fatwa attributed to Ayatollah Khamenei) allowed donor gametes. Confirm, and whether to name.
End of life: euthanasia forbidden; withdrawing futile treatment allowed by some (e.g. OIC academy rulings): confirm. Brain death debate open.
'Jurists of Baghdad and Cordoba' is illustrative; hospital scene is illustrative.
